_doc: Mining districts outside the reference empire, plus tags that complete the fuel and metal shares. share_of_reference_output is a district's share of the reference civilisation's output of that resource (the empire total that data/world/resources.json gives for the metals), and is how much of the resource a holder of the tile, or a buyer within reach of it, can draw on; it is read by sim/world/mineral_shares.py and never enters the supply curve of the reference empire (that is share_of_empire_output on the Roman-world rows). Every share here is a temporary_heuristic: no district-level production series exists in the sources named, so each figure is the rough relative abundance the former region table gave, now sited at one named district. A resource counts as tracked when any row of it carries this field. conf describes the location and the source, not the share. No endowment is given where none could be defended.

entries.name: Scania Coalfield
entries.source: Skane (Sweden) coal measures around Hoganas and Bjuv, the Nordic region's small coalfield, worked from the late eighteenth century; location from the Geological Survey of Sweden's description of the Rhaetian-Jurassic coal-bearing beds.

entries.name: Bergslagen Iron District
entries.source: Bergslagen (Dalarna, Vastmanland, Orebro), the central Swedish ore district whose bloomery iron was smelted from the Iron Age and exported as osmund iron in the Middle Ages.

entries.name: Sala Lead Mine
entries.source: Sala silver-lead mine, Vastmanland, worked from the fifteenth century at the latest; the galena carries the silver. Position from the Swedish national heritage listing of the mine.

entries.name: Sala Silver Mine
entries.source: Sala silver mine, Vastmanland, Sweden's chief silver producer from the late Middle Ages; the same working as the lead entry, listed once per metal.

entries.name: Magan Copper (Oman)
entries.source: Wadi Jizzi and Lasail copper of the Semail ophiolite, smelted from the third millennium BC (Magan of the cuneiform texts); Weisgerber's excavations of the Oman copper smelting sites.

entries.name: Mahd adh Dhahab
entries.source: Mahd adh Dhahab ('Cradle of Gold'), Hejaz, an ancient gold, silver and copper working; Luce, O'Neil and Rye, Mahd adh Dhahab: Precambrian epithermal gold deposit in Saudi Arabia, US Geological Survey Open-File Report 78-388 (1978), https://pubs.usgs.gov/publication/ofr78388. Silver is a minor product.

entries.name: Wadi Sawawin Iron
entries.source: Wadi Sawawin banded iron formation, Midyan terrane of northwest Saudi Arabia, about 60 km from the Red Sea port of Duba; the one large iron body of the peninsula. No ancient working is attested, so this share is a placeholder for the peninsula's small iron output. Position approximate (no published coordinate found).

entries.name: Konasamudram Iron (Deccan)
entries.source: Konasamudram and Nirmal (Telangana), the Deccan centre where wootz crucible steel was made from local ores; Craddock on early Indian iron and steel. Share for the subcontinent's iron.

entries.name: Khetri Copper Belt
entries.source: Khetri-Singhana belt, Rajasthan, copper worked since the Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture (Ganeshwar site, Wikipedia); Willies, Ancient and post-medieval mining sites in the Khetri copper belt and the Kolar gold field, India, Bulletin of the Peak District Mines Historical Society 11(6), 1992, 285-295, listed in the Heritage of Metals and Societies review of Indian metallurgy but not read here. No joint Hegde and Craddock work on Khetri was found.

entries.name: Hazaribagh Tin
entries.source: Cassiterite of the Hazaribagh-Gaya mica belt, Bihar-Jharkhand, as a placeholder for the small Indian tin output. No source found for tin in Hazaribagh or Gaya (Indian Bureau of Mines Bihar listings omit tin; India's commercial cassiterite is in Bastar and Dantewada, Chhattisgarh), so the occurrence is unverified. Ancient India imported most of its tin.

entries.name: Zawar Lead
entries.source: Zawar, Udaipur, Rajasthan: lead-zinc-silver mines with a Mauryan-period phase (radiocarbon on mine timbers, late first millennium BC) and a second phase from the fourteenth century, where medieval zinc distillation was practised; Craddock and Hegde, Early Indian Metallurgy (Zawar, Agucha, Dariba), https://esamskriti.com/e/Culture/Indian-Culture/ZINC-Mining-in-Zawar-region-of-Rajasthan~Interview-with-Dr.-Paul-T.-Craddock-1.aspx.

entries.name: Zawar Silver
entries.source: Zawar, Rajasthan: silver from the argentiferous galena, as the lead entry; Craddock and Hegde, Early Indian Metallurgy. Silver recovery here is not independently re-checked.

entries.name: Choghart-Chadormalu Iron
entries.source: Choghart iron oxide deposit, Bafq district (Yazd), about 12 km northeast of Bafq, with Chadormalu 80 km to the north; a large Precambrian iron body. Medieval working is not independently verified.

entries.name: Anarak Copper
entries.source: Talmessi and Meskani copper-nickel-cobalt ores, Anarak district, Iran; Encyclopaedia Iranica (Copper ii, Copper resources in Iran; Anarak) gives Talmessi as a possible early native-copper mine and Anarak copper mining as probably pre-Islamic, so Bronze Age working here is not confirmed. Kerman's Sar Cheshmeh is the larger modern body.

entries.name: Mushiston Tin
entries.source: Mushiston copper-tin deposit, Kaznok valley of the Zeravshan mountains about 35 km south of Penjikent (Tajikistan), mined from the end of the third millennium BC; Karnab, Lapas and Changali (Uzbekistan) lie farther west and are not covered by this point. Cierny, Weisgerber and Parzinger on Central Asian tin; Frontiers in Earth Science 2023, doi 10.3389/feart.2023.1224873. Position approximate.

entries.name: Karamazar Lead
entries.source: Karamazar range (Kan-i-Mansur), Tajikistan and Uzbekistan: mining and smelting of the ninth to eleventh centuries is attested at the Mansura mine (Wikipedia, Mining in Tajikistan); the geographers' accounts of it were not checked. Position approximate.

entries.name: Karamazar Silver
entries.source: Karamazar range (Kan-i-Mansur): silver mines of the Samanid period, as the lead entry; Transoxianan silver feeding Samanid dirhams is argued in the Journal of Historical Research (jhr.usb.ac.ir/article_9357). Position approximate.

entries.name: Handan-Wu'an Iron
entries.source: Handan-Wu'an (Hebei) skarn iron district; Han state ironworks such as Tieshenggou (Henan, about 200 km southwest) are described in Wagner, Iron and Steel in Ancient China (Brill, 1993), which does not itself source the Handan ore. Ore source is not independently verified.

entries.name: Tonglushan Copper
entries.source: Tonglushan, Daye (Hubei), the best-excavated ancient copper mine in China, worked from the Shang-Zhou period for over a millennium; Hubei Provincial Museum excavation reports.

entries.name: Gejiu Tin
entries.source: Gejiu (Yunnan): earliest clear working there is copper from the Han period and tin was mined on a large scale only from the early 1900s; long tin exploitation is probable but not proven (Heidelberg Sinology mining project, https://www.zo.uni-heidelberg.de/sinologie/research/epm/09_gejiu.html). Yunnan deposits are reported as China's main Han tin source (Wikipedia, Tin mining).

entries.name: Shuikoushan Lead
entries.source: Shuikoushan (Changning, Hunan), a lead-zinc-copper district; Qing-period Hunan lead mining is covered by Lin Rongqin on Hunan mining, but Shuikoushan's own early history was not found. Date of first working unverified.

entries.name: Huize Silver
entries.source: Huize and the Yunnan silver mines: Yunnan was the most productive silver region from the Yuan onward, Ming records name about twenty mines and Qing records about two hundred, and the Jinniu mines at Huize were productive from the late 1780s (Heidelberg Sinology mining project, https://www.zo.uni-heidelberg.de/sinologie/research/epm/12_jinniu_huize.html). Von Glahn, Fountain of Fortune (1996), covers the Ming-Qing silver economy but was not found to treat Huize.

entries.name: Taruga-Nok Iron
entries.source: Taruga and the Nok culture (central Nigeria), among the earliest iron smelting in West Africa, from the middle of the first millennium BC; Fagg Rackham, Franke, Junius, Maennel and Beck, Early West African Iron Smelting: The Legacy of Taruga in Light of Recent Nok Research, African Archaeological Review (2017), doi 10.1007/s10437-017-9262-2.

entries.name: Akjoujt Copper
entries.source: Akjoujt (Mauritania), copper mined and smelted in the first millennium BC at the Grotte aux Chauves-souris mine (radiocarbon dates reported by Courcier and colleagues, CUPRUM project, citing Lambert 1965 and 1975; Killick 1988 cites Lambert 1971 and 1983 for mid first millennium BC smelting). The title and journal of Lambert 1971 (Les industries sur cuivre dans l'Ouest saharien) were not verified. Medieval working not verified.

entries.name: Thai Nguyen Iron
entries.source: Trai Cau and Thai Nguyen iron of northern Vietnam (Geological Survey of Vietnam); iron smelting spread to Dong Son and Oc Eo cultures from the late first millennium BC. Position approximate.

entries.name: Khao Wong Prachan Copper
entries.source: Khao Wong Prachan valley (Lopburi, Thailand), Bronze Age copper mining and smelting; Pigott and Natapintu, Thailand's early copper-base metallurgy.

entries.name: Copperbelt Silver
entries.source: Silver won as a minor by-product of the Central African Copperbelt; no ancient silver mining is attested in the region. The share stands for the region's small silver output.

entries.name: Nizhny Tagil Iron (Urals)
entries.source: Mount Vysokaya and Gora Blagodat, central Urals, the magnetite behind the Demidov Nizhny Tagil ironworks (begun 1725); Hudson, The Rise of the Demidov Family and the Russian Iron Industry in the Eighteenth Century (Oriental Research Partners, 1986).

entries.name: Gumeshevsk Copper (Urals)
entries.source: Gumeshevskoye (Gumyoshevsky) mine, Polevskoy, Urals: copper in use from the mid second millennium BC (Wikipedia, Gumyoshevsky mine) and a source of Final Bronze Age copper for Itkul and Sarmatian cultures (Ankusheva and colleagues); deposit found 1702, Polevskoy copper smelter 1724 to 1930. Chud and Demidov attributions are not sourced.

entries.name: Zmeinogorsk Lead (Altai)
entries.source: Zmeinogorsk and the Rudny Altai polymetallic ores, with ancient workings and the Demidov-founded Kolyvan-Voskresensk works (1727); silver ore discovered in winter 1743.

entries.name: Zmeinogorsk Silver (Altai)
entries.source: Zmeinogorsk Altai silver, the same ore as the lead entry; first Altai silver was presented in 1744 and the works passed to the Crown for it.

entries.name: Cerro de Mercado Iron
entries.source: Cerro de Mercado (Durango), a large hematite-magnetite hill; the pre-Hispanic Americas used iron ore for mirrors and pigment but did not smelt it. The share stands for that small output.

entries.name: Inguaran Copper (Michoacan)
entries.source: Inguaran, Michoacan, a copper source of West Mexican metallurgy, which began after about AD 700 along the Ecuador-Peru maritime route; Hosler, The Sounds and Colors of Power (MIT Press, 1994) and Hosler and Macfarlane, Copper Sources, Metal Production and Metals Trade in Late Postclassic Mesoamerica, Science 273 (1996) 1819-1824. Inguaran itself is not named in any source found, so its place among the sampled ores is unverified.

entries.name: Taxco Tin
entries.source: Small cassiterite occurrences in the Taxco-Guerrero belt may have supplied tin bronze in prehispanic Mexico (Hosler); not verified. Position approximate.

entries.name: Zimapan Lead
entries.source: Zimapan (Hidalgo), a lead-silver-zinc district worked from the sixteenth century on older native workings.

entries.name: Taxco Silver
entries.source: Taxco, Guerrero, early Spanish silver mines of the 1530s (Encyclopedia.com, Taxco; Wikipedia, Taxco gives about 1532) and part of the Mexican silver belt with Zacatecas; Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico: Zacatecas 1546-1700 (Cambridge University Press, 1971) covers Zacatecas, not Taxco.

entries.name: Oruro-Potosi Tin
entries.source: Oruro and the Bolivian tin belt, a candidate source of Andean tin bronze: tin bronze appears in northern Bolivia in the Tiwanaku period, and Lechtman and Macfarlane's lead isotope work places Tiwanaku bronze ores in the Bolivian puna and high sierra, but no source found names Oruro as the prehispanic tin source. Unverified.

entries.name: Cerro de Pasco Lead
entries.source: Cerro de Pasco, Peru, a lead-zinc-silver district worked from the colonial period on pre-Inca workings.

entries.name: Keweenaw Native Copper
entries.source: Keweenaw Peninsula and Isle Royale, Michigan: native copper mined by the Old Copper Complex peoples; lake-sediment geochemistry dates Isle Royale mining to 6500 to 5400 years ago, Pompeani et al., The Holocene (2014), doi 10.1177/0959683614557574.

entries.name: Mesabi Iron Range
entries.source: Mesabi Range (Minnesota), the Lake Superior taconite and iron ore district that supplied the industrial United States from 1892.

entries.name: Upper Mississippi Valley Lead
entries.source: Galena-Dubuque lead-zinc district, worked by Native Americans for galena and by Euro-Americans from the 1820s; US Geological Survey.

entries.name: Cobalt Native Silver (Ontario)
entries.source: Cobalt-Gowganda district, Ontario, rich native silver found in 1903; native silver also occurs with Keweenaw copper.
entries.working_unknown: UNKNOWN (B): the source gives the discovery (1903) but no endowment was read, so neither a working date nor a size is stated here

entries.name: Burra Copper
entries.source: Burra (South Australia), the first big Australian copper mine, opened 1845; no pre-colonial copper working.

entries.name: Isua Iron Belt (Greenland)
entries.source: Isukasia banded iron formation, southwest Greenland (Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland); the Norse bog-iron working was tiny, hence a small share.

entries.name: Bihar-Bengal Saltpetre Earths
entries.source: Saran, Tirhut and Patna districts on the Gangetic plain: potassium nitrate leached from efflorescent soils, the world's main saltpetre supply from the 1600s; Buchanan, Hamilton and East India Company records.

entries.name: Iranian Nitre Earths
entries.source: Nitre earths of the Iranian plateau (Khorasan, Kerman, Yazd) leached for saltpetre in the Safavid period. Position approximate.

entries.name: Shanxi Nitre Earths
entries.source: Chinese xiao shi was gathered from nitre earths in north China (Shanxi, Shaanxi) and Sichuan; Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol 5, part 7. Position approximate.
